title: Forensic DNA Markers: Autosomal STRs, Y-STRs and Mitochondrial DNA
summary: Explain how autosomal STR profiles achieve individual identification (CODIS), and when lineage markers — Y-STRs and mtDNA — are chosen and how their matches must be reported.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 74 Hits 1, 8 and 10 and Traps 2 and 3 (first lesson for Ch. 74), with mtDNA as comparison. Checked against Nwawuba 2020, Syndercombe Court 2021 (Y chromosome; mtDNA). Not taught: “20 loci commonly rarer than 1 in 1 nonillion” (Hit 1), mtDNA “discriminatory power ~1 in a few thousand” and homoplasmy (Hit 4 — Hit 4 not counted as covered), STR repeat-unit size 3–7 nt (Hit 3) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Explain how independent STR loci produce very small random match probabilities.
Contrast autosomal STR, Y-STR and mtDNA inheritance and discriminating power.
Choose the marker system for a sample and report lineage matches correctly.

scenes.title: Three samples, three marker systems
scenes.altText: Three invented casework samples: (1) a cigarette butt with ample DNA; (2) a sexual-assault swab where the victim’s DNA vastly outweighs a small amount of male DNA; (3) a shed hair with no root and old skeletal remains. Question token: “Which marker system fits each — and how much does a match prove?”

cues.text: Three samples reach the forensic lab: a cigarette butt with plenty of DNA, and a sexual-assault swab where a little male DNA is swamped by the victim’s.
The third is a shed hair without a root, plus old bones.
Which marker system suits each, and how much does a match really prove?

props.label: Which markers? How much does a match prove?

scenes.title: Autosomal STRs: counting repeats
scenes.altText: STR card (Nwawuba 2020): short tandem repeats are highly polymorphic; alleles differ in the number of repeat units, which change by strand slippage and unequal crossing over; inherited from both parents and assorted independently. CODIS card: the US database used 13 core loci — with all 13, the average random match probability is rarer than 1 in a trillion among unrelated individuals; in January 2017 new CODIS profiles expanded to 21 markers including the sex marker amelogenin (20 STR loci). Amelogenin targets a gene on X and Y (AMELY) to indicate sex.

cues.text: Autosomal short tandem repeats, STRs, are short DNA motifs repeated in a row. People differ in how many repeats they carry at each locus.
Repeat numbers change through strand slippage and unequal crossing over, and each locus is inherited from both parents independently, so combining loci multiplies the rarity.
With all 13 original CODIS core loci, the average random match probability is rarer than one in a trillion among unrelated people.
In January 2017, new CODIS profiles expanded to 21 markers, 20 STR loci plus the sex marker amelogenin.

scenes.title: Lineage markers: Y-STR and mtDNA
scenes.altText: Y-STR card (Syndercombe Court 2021, Y chromosome): Y-STRs form a single haplotype passed from father to son; they do not give near-certain individual identification — relatives on the paternal line share the haplotype — but they are valuable in sexual-assault cases where male DNA is small relative to female DNA. They cannot prove paternity but can help when a putative father is absent (paternal relatives). mtDNA card (Syndercombe Court 2021, mtDNA): 16,569-bp circular genome, inherited through the maternal line; a noncoding ~1,121-bp control region (D-loop) holds the hypervariable regions; high copy number makes it useful for bones, teeth and hair and in disaster victim identification; a haplotype identifies a maternal lineage, not an individual; rarity is estimated by counting in databases.

cues.text: Y-chromosome STRs are inherited together as one haplotype from father to son. All men on the same paternal line share it, so a Y-STR match cannot identify one individual with near certainty.
Their strength is sexual-assault evidence, where a little male DNA is swamped by female DNA: Y-STRs see only the male.
Mitochondrial DNA is a 16,569 base-pair circle inherited through the maternal line. Most variation lies in the noncoding control region, the D-loop.
Because each cell holds many copies, mtDNA works for bones, teeth and hair with little nuclear DNA. But it identifies a maternal lineage, not a person.

scenes.title: Matching the sample to the marker
scenes.altText: Comparison card: autosomal STR — individual identification (RMP < 1 in a trillion with 13 loci) but needs adequate nuclear DNA; Y-STR — male-specific, lineage-level, ideal for male DNA in a female background; mtDNA — maternal lineage, high copy number for degraded/limited samples, least individualizing. Back to the hook: cigarette butt → autosomal STR (CODIS); assault swab → Y-STRs (and autosomal STRs on any separated male fraction); hair shaft/old bones → mtDNA. Reporting token: a Y-STR or mtDNA match means “same lineage”, never “same person”.

cues.text: Autosomal STRs give individual identification, but they need enough nuclear DNA.
Y-STRs are male-specific and lineage-level, ideal for male DNA hidden in a female background.
Mitochondrial DNA works on limited or degraded samples, but is the least individualizing.
Back to the samples: cigarette butt, autosomal STRs for CODIS. Assault swab, Y-STRs. Hair shaft and old bones, mitochondrial DNA.
And report carefully: a Y-STR or mtDNA match means the same lineage, never the same person.

props.label: Lineage match = same lineage, not same person

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “mtDNA is more discriminating because there are thousands of copies” (✓ copy number helps sensitivity, not discrimination — mtDNA identifies a maternal lineage); “A Y-STR match is as strong as an autosomal profile” (✓ shared by paternal relatives; lineage-level); “More loci don’t matter once you have a few” (✓ independent loci multiply rarity — 13 CODIS loci < 1 in a trillion).

cues.text: Trap one: mtDNA is more discriminating because each cell has thousands of copies. Copy number improves sensitivity, not discrimination; mtDNA identifies a maternal lineage.
Trap two: a Y-STR match is as strong as an autosomal profile. Paternal relatives share the same Y haplotype, so it is lineage-level evidence.
Trap three: a few loci are as good as many. Independent loci multiply rarity; all 13 original CODIS loci give a match probability rarer than one in a trillion.

scenes.title: Person, Pa, Ma
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Autosomal finds the Person; Y finds the Pa’s line; mito finds the Ma’s line.” Tokens: STR = person · Y-STR = father’s line · mtDNA = mother’s line. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: autosomal STRs find the person; Y-STRs find the father’s line; mitochondrial DNA finds the mother’s line.
Where it breaks: identical twins share autosomal profiles; heteroplasmy can complicate mtDNA comparisons; and rapidly mutating Y-STRs can sometimes separate close paternal relatives.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Autosomal STRs: repeat counts at independent loci · 13 CODIS loci RMP < 1 in a trillion · 2017: 20 STRs + amelogenin”, “Y-STR = paternal haplotype (male DNA in female excess) · mtDNA = 16,569 bp maternal lineage, high copy (bones, hair) · lineage ≠ individual”.

cues.text: Autosomal STRs identify individuals by multiplying the rarity of independent repeat loci, while Y-STRs and mitochondrial DNA identify only paternal or maternal lineages but succeed where autosomal typing cannot.

props.label: Autosomal STR: 13 CODIS loci RMP < 1 in a trillion · 2017: 20 STRs + amelogenin
Y-STR = paternal line · mtDNA = maternal line, high copy · lineage ≠ person

explanation.what: Plain language: forensic labs compare DNA regions that vary between people; ordinary (autosomal) repeat markers can point to one person, while Y-chromosome and mitochondrial markers follow family lines and are used when the sample is mixed or degraded. Scientific terms: short tandem repeat (STR), locus, allele (repeat number), random match probability (RMP), CODIS, amelogenin, Y-STR haplotype, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), control region (D-loop), hypervariable region, lineage marker.
explanation.why: Each autosomal STR locus is inherited from both parents and assorts independently, so genotype frequencies multiply across loci. The Y chromosome passes intact from father to son and mtDNA from mother to children, so all members of a lineage share the same haplotype; mtDNA’s high copy number makes it recoverable from bones, teeth and hair.
explanation.measure: All 13 original CODIS loci: average RMP rarer than 1 in a trillion among unrelated individuals; since January 2017 new CODIS profiles use 21 markers including amelogenin (Nwawuba 2020). mtDNA 16,569 bp; ~1,121-bp noncoding control region with hypervariable regions; maternal inheritance; rarity estimated by database counting (Syndercombe Court 2021). Y-STR haplotype father-to-son; valuable for male DNA in female excess; cannot prove paternity (Syndercombe Court 2021).
explanation.differs: Autosomal STR (individual, biparental) vs Y-STR (paternal lineage, male-specific) vs mtDNA (maternal lineage, high copy number).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: why mtDNA or Y-STRs are less discriminating, which marker for a sexual-assault swab or a hair shaft, and CODIS loci facts.

questions.stem: A sexual-assault swab contains a small amount of male DNA in a large excess of the victim’s DNA. Which marker system best targets the male contributor?

options.rationale: Correct. Y-STRs detect only male DNA, valuable when male material is small relative to female DNA.
Incorrect. The victim’s mtDNA would dominate and mtDNA is not male-specific.
Incorrect. Amelogenin indicates sex but does not identify the contributor.
Incorrect. The female profile would overwhelm the small male component.

questions.stem: Why is an mtDNA match less individualizing than an autosomal STR match?

options.text: mtDNA is inherited as one maternal haplotype shared by the whole maternal lineage
options.rationale: Correct. A haplotype identifies a lineage, not an individual.

options.text: mtDNA has too few copies per cell
options.rationale: Incorrect. mtDNA has high copy number — that is why it works on bones and hair.
Incorrect. mtDNA is maternally inherited and lacks recombination of the kind autosomes undergo.
Incorrect. The control region and whole mitogenome can be sequenced.

questions.stem: With all 13 original CODIS core loci typed, what is the average random match probability among unrelated individuals?

options.rationale: Correct. Independent loci multiply genotype frequencies.
Incorrect. That is far too common for a 13-locus profile.
Incorrect. 13 loci give much rarer match probabilities.
Incorrect. Match probabilities are estimates; identical twins share profiles.
